title: Breaking And Entering: Dry Cleaning On Their Latest Album 'Secret Love'
transcript:
Florence Shaw and Lewis Maynard of Dry Cleaning spoke with Billy, just after the band's UK tour, about their new album Secret Love. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 22 January 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Billy: They've just done a UK tour, playing songs from the new album, which came out at the start of January, for the first time. This is Flo on how the shows have been going.

Flo: Really good. We were saying yesterday that people seem to have gelled with them really quickly. Sometimes you play new stuff for a long, long time before you get that kind of recognition from the audience, before people really start to feel it. But we found that super quickly with these songs. I'm not sure why. Maybe there's an immediacy to them that's a bit more sticky than the songs on Stumpwork or something like that, which are more of a slow-burn kind of vibe. But it's been great. It's been really nice.

Billy: That's actually a really interesting point, because your songs typically don't have conventional choruses or obvious hooks, although there are maybe some more conventional-esque choruses on this record. Lewis, when you finished making it, did you have a sense that it would be more immediate for listeners?

Lewis: No, it's really hard to judge. It's almost impossible to judge how it goes down. Your expectations always get flipped. Something you think was going to work in the studio might not work in the studio, but kind of works live. Something that works in the studio doesn't always work live.

So it's always a pleasant surprise, and it's one of my favourite things about the whole recording process: your expectations flip, but how you hear the songs flips as well. When you demo a song, it sounds to us a certain way. Then when we show it to someone, it instantly sounds different. When we record it, it actually sounds different. And when it becomes public, it sounds different again. You submit it to the world, and then the song sounds different to yourself too.

Billy: That is super interesting. This record seems fairly collaborative: internally you seem to be a very collaborative band, and then there's demoing with Gilla Band, working with Cate Le Bon, from what I've read, and getting some input from Jason from Sleaford Mods. Flo, is reaching out to people outside the band helpful for gauging whether songs are working or making an impression?

Flo: It can be. It tells you quite interesting things sometimes. We showed our demos to Jason, and he would immediately pick up on certain lines, or just get really excited about certain lines. He'd either laugh out loud, or he'd want to hear it again, or he'd say, 'Oh, you should say that again at the end of the song,' or, 'That should come at the start of a verse. It's such a great line.'

It's not that I necessarily followed that advice word for word, but it's just really interesting, because obviously the lyrics are so personal to me. Things that mean a lot to me, or things that I find really funny, are not always the same for somebody coming to it totally fresh. So it's just intriguing. It's like an experiment or something. It's like a lab or something, where watching his reactions was so interesting and quite freeing in a way.

It really reduced the pressure somehow just to show it to somebody, but someone who I knew kind of knew what it was like to write and perform a little bit in the way that I do. He was a really valuable person to chat to, actually.

Billy: That's interesting, that you used the word pressure. Did you feel much pressure making this album?

Flo: I think amongst ourselves we're always trying to impress each other, which is a bit of a cliché, but it is true. I don't think we often think about the audience necessarily until this point. It's always like you want to — I mean, it sounds so wholesome — but you want to do your best, because we're each striving quite a bit to write good stuff and to push ourselves. So you want to meet that level.

I mean, it would be — sorry, Lewis.

Lewis: No, I was going to say there's never a moment where it's kind of, 'Now we start writing.' We're always jamming, and there's always such a bank of ideas. I said it maybe this time last year, or maybe even a bit earlier: songs that will be on the record, we've already written. We just don't know it yet. They're just in an iPhone recording somewhere. That's always the way. It could be just a lyric, or a guitar part, or a synth part. It could be anything. It's just sat somewhere.

And a lot of the writing comes from listening back to jams we've had, so there's not that pressure of, 'Now you're doing it.' There are also songs on the record, one in particular, which we started writing in a previous studio session. So you never know when ideas are going to come; that's one of the exciting parts as well. I call it fishing. You could be having the worst day in the studio, but if there's 30 seconds of a good idea at the end, you get to run with that, which is really fun.

Billy: That's a good reminder to keep showing up, even if you're not feeling it.

Lewis: That's so true. Every time someone's like, 'I feel a bit tired. Should we just go home?' we're like, 'No, because this is when the good stuff normally comes.'

Billy: You were saying you want to do your best, which is a good sign. If you didn't care about what was coming out at this stage, you'd probably do something else. Secret Love, to my eyes, is the broadest and most dynamic of your three albums, and also the most melodic, with some really pretty moments. Were you conscious of not limiting yourselves in the sorts of song ideas you would explore?

Flo: I think maybe, yeah. But I think it's interesting: we never really think about that, I guess. We have such a specific sound, but it feels like that's come about just because of who we each are, rather than something really conscious that we're trying to do. Sometimes we write things that don't really sound like us, but then somehow they always come around and end up sounding like Dry Cleaning.

We had days where Tom would just bring in a keyboard and not play guitar at all, and there's a song called 'I Need You' that came from a day like that. It feels like that would break down a lot of what we sound like, in a way, but it still didn't. Lewis was saying the other day that maybe the answer to why we sound like we sound is that we're all just really stubborn, and we don't move very far towards each other. We just do our own thing and refuse to adapt or change, even if it would be easier if we did. Even if going in the direction one person's pulling in would make a more cohesive song, we still don't do it.

Lewis: We once had a producer who tried to get me and Tom to play in sync, and we were like, 'Why would you do that?' Everyone was really upset.

Billy: In the whole Dry Cleaning project there seems to be a question of, 'Will this work?', with all of you doing your individual things, like you're describing, and you keep finding ways for the answer to be yes. It's not obvious who's leading. The relationship between the bass and the guitar is very lateral: it's not just open chords and root notes, it's really interesting harmony. And the way you sing, and the way your lyrics flow, isn't an obvious fit for the music.

Lewis: No, yeah. There's a surprising amount of space for everyone. Even though everyone's very stubborn, everyone's very respectful about giving other people space to explore whatever their instrument is doing at that time. Everyone swaps roles, giving someone else the chance to do a melody, or doing the melody themselves, or being more rhythmic. You're always jamming off each other.

So I always say that we always jam off Flo's vocals. And even if you can't really hear the words in the rehearsal, because it sounds so bad in there, you can kind of hear the rhythms of what she's saying, so you get to kind of roll against that. So even though there's stubbornness, there's also a respect for boundaries, about going into other people's areas.

Billy: Flo, to ask you about working with Cate Le Bon: you made your first couple of albums with John Parish, who's no mug either, but it's very cool that you worked with Cate Le Bon, and from everything I've read you're very fond of her and her music, and of the experience of working with her. When you listen to the album, do you recognise a lot of her input?

Flo: Totally. Doing vocals with her was such a great experience. We did them on our own: she shooed everyone out of the studio, and we would spend the mornings, about three or four hours every morning, doing vocals. Doing, say, three takes of a song and then listening through to them all in the control room and choosing, comping them together, that sort of thing.

That was such a great experience, because she has a very good mix of that fondness for detail, but also not having too much patience for being really pernickety about things. I can get so tied up in tiny, tiny, tiny details that it's not very helpful, and she's really good at saying, 'Now, that'll do,' at the right moment. And with a vocal that's imperfect, she puts a lot of value on that.

So she changes her dial, in a way, from looking at tiny, tiny details to really broad strokes, which makes for very human-sounding records, I think. Whereas I can just focus down to a level that's a bit crackers. So we were a good foil for each other in that way. And she just cared so much about the emotional quality of the performances, which is really important to me in the fairly small spectrum that I operate in.

She really cared about that, the intensity of certain parts, but also when it's more about rhythm than emotion. She was just really attuned to all of that. I didn't really have to explain any of it. It was just great. I could do vocals with her all day, every day.

Lewis: It's also worth saying that this didn't happen with John, because with John we recorded almost everything live together. But so often when you're in a studio, you spend so much time tracking everything, and then you're like, 'Cool, so we've got about 10 minutes left today. Should we go do the vocals?' And that would be it, at the last minute, for such a huge part, such an important part.

Billy: That happens across the board, doesn't it? Vocals are always last, and for good reasons, but it's a bit scary, I guess.

Flo: The same was with John. He had a lot of time for my attention to detail, which I love him forever for. He was up for listening to three different versions of the word 'Armani' or whatever, which was a lot of words he'd probably never heard in songs before.
